headlines.title: Former Santa Clara County undersheriff pleads guilty in bribery scheme
headlines.description: A political corruption scandal in the South Bay has concluded with a felony conviction. Former Santa Clara County Undersheriff Rick Sung pleaded guilty to two felony bribery charges, admitting that he ran a pay-to-play scheme out of the sheriff’s office. Prosecutors say Sung weaponized his power by trading highly coveted, rarely issued concealed weapons permits for luxury corporate perks. The bribes included hundreds of Apple iPads and access to a luxury suite for San Jose Sharks games at the SAP Center. The guilty plea closes an eight-year corruption probe that led to several convictions and forced former Sheriff Laurie Smith out of office. Under the terms of the resolution, Sung must complete 400 hours of community service and permanently surrender his California law enforcement badge.

headlines.title: SFUSD parents press for AI policy in classrooms after Dreamforce remarks
headlines.description: The role of artificial intelligence in San Francisco Unified School District classrooms is drawing questions from parents following comments made by the district’s superintendent at the Dreamforce conference last week. Parents say they want to be more involved in shaping the district’s policy on AI in class. During her comments at Dreamforce last week, SFUSD Superintendent Maria Su was careful not to specifically say “AI” or “artificial intelligence.” Instead, she described “technology” and “tools” that will help in the classroom of the future. “We need to support educators to learn how to use tools. To learn how to use technology in the safest way possible. But in order to do this we need to understand the tools,” Su said. Last week, Salesforce also announced $18 million in education grants to school districts in San Francisco, Oakland and three other cities, specifically to support continued learning in AI. SFUSD has already approved a couple of AI-supported applications in classrooms. Amira is an AI reading tutor, and ChatGPT Edu has been deployed to 12,000 students and teachers across the district. Members of the San Francisco Parents Coalition say there are several concerns about artificial intelligence in classrooms and want the district to tread carefully. “One, is student safety. Especially at a young age. Our children’s likenesses, their faces, their voices being recorded, is something that needs to be thought through,” said Rebecca Kee, executive director of the SF Parents Coalition. Kee says there are also concerns about older students becoming dependent on tools like chatbots or other AI agents. Adults also need to be ahead of the AI curve, and parents are concerned they are not. “The district already has a lot on its plate, so understandably parents are wondering, how can they keep track of all of these tools, and all the things they can do, and meanwhile, keep children safe, and support their learning with them. It’s a lot to take on,” Kee added. The union representing teachers has also raised concerns about tools like Amira for adding to educators’ workloads rather than helping relieve it. Right now, the district does not have a policy on AI use. Instead, individual schools are adopting guidelines and practices. But composing a districtwide policy is in progress, so the parents coalition is encouraging parents to become part of that effort. The Board of Commissioners is scheduled to vote on that new policy next March.

headlines.title: Sierra LaMar murder case: Defense in retrial requests judge to recuse himself
headlines.description: The defense team in the retrial for the man convicted of kidnapping and killing Morgan Hill teenager Sierra LaMar is calling the judge biased and requesting he recuse himself. The surprising move on Monday comes weeks before the start of Antolin Garcia-Torres’s retrial. His defense team argues the judge was biased based on a handful of prior rulings and because he used to work as a prosecutor in Santa Clara County. “To make this move now, I think, is very unusual,” said Steven Clark, a legal analyst. “It may be that they’re trying to work the refs like you see coaches do in sports. That they’re trying to say, ‘Look, some of these rulings have not gone our way. We hope we’ll get some rulings down the road.’ I don’t think this is going to be successful.” Judge Brian Buckelew said as prosecutor he had never worked directly on the Sierra LaMar case. He also gave an important tentative ruling that favored the defense, saying he was inclined to now allow prosecutors to use the DNA data firm Cybergenetics for potential analysis. “This case will come down to the DNA evidence and the validity of the way it was gathered and tested,” Clark said. “Having the prosecution not be able to use the DNA experts they want is a huge win for the defense.” Morgan Hill Apr 27 Morgan Hill Mar 2 Morgan Hill Feb 27 The 15-year-old LaMar vanished in March 2012 while on her way to school in Morgan Hill and her body was never found. Her cell phone and belongings were later discovered on the side of the road two miles from her home, containing trace evidence that tied Garcia-Torres to her disappearance. Her DNA was also found in Garcia-Torres’s car. But without a body, murder weapon, or crime scene, that forensic DNA was the crux of the Santa Clara County District Attorney’s case. In June 2017, Garcia-Torres was sentenced to life for her murder. A judge in February overturned the conviction, partly because the district attorney had used three unrelated kidnapping cases to help convict Garcia-Torres. Garcia-Torres has remained in prison. Both sides are set to return to court Thursday. The judge in that hearing is expected to rule whether he plans to stay on the case.

headlines.title: California declares state of emergency as state braces for super El Niño storms
headlines.description: California is bracing for a “Super El Niño” that some believe could bring some of the strongest storms, and storm damage, the state has ever seen. Gov. Gavin Newsom considers the warning so dire that he has declared a preemptive state of emergency. Folks who live along the Russian River in Guerneville are no strangers to flooding, but tonight they are gearing up for possible record conditions. “Comes in fast and then it drains by the tides. The tides hold the water the creek can’t get out,” said Steven Cline, a Guerneville resident who describes the flooding that takes place in his neighborhood nearly every year. But Cline says he is now gearing up for potentially historic flooding.California officials are sounding the alarm, saying a record-breaking El Niño could bring extreme storms and flooding across the state. “The risk in front of us is serious. This is part of a larger and alarming trend,” said Caroline Thomas Jacobs, director of the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services. Thomas Jacobs added that climate-driven El Niño conditions could mean months of dangerous weather, heavy rain, strong winds, deep mountain snow, and flooding, emphasizing that Californians should understand this clearly. Paul Lowenthal with the Santa Rosa Fire Department says that while it is unclear whether the forecasted El Niño conditions will hold, the emergency declaration is a great reminder to prepare. “Whether it’s knowing when to sign up for emergency alerts, having your go-bag ready, being prepared for the potential of outages, being prepared to evacuate at a moment’s notice,” Lowenthal said. State and local officials are already gearing up. Cal Fire crews have been removing trees along River Road in Sonoma County — trees at risk of coming down in a big storm. They are clearing debris from waterways and getting ready to put in extra sandbag stations. They are also prepositioning California National Guard equipment, including high-water vehicles to be used for water rescues if needed. “Last couple weeks they were sledging the creek, taking all the debris, taking out 100 yards of dirt, bulldozer, bulldoze tree debris, garbage and clearing all culverts out, so they’re preparing for it,” Cline said. Cline says he is glad to see the state and the county taking precautions. He says he will start moving his belongings to higher ground soon. “El Niño is going to really sock us this year, so I’m preparing, that’s all I can do,” he added. headlines.title: Air district report links Richmond Chevron refinery emissions to elevated health risks
headlines.description: Bay Area air quality officials met with Richmond residents to discuss a preliminary health risk assessment that indicates emissions from the Chevron refinery pose potential health risks to parts of the city. Officials emphasized that the assessment is not an immediate warning for residents to stay indoors, but the findings identify risks high enough to potentially require corrective action from Chevron. The report estimates a maximum lifetime cancer risk of 37 in a million from refinery emissions — more than three times the district’s threshold. It also identified short-term non-cancer health risks exceeding district standards. “10 out of 266 of different sources throughout the refinery were found to be above the limit that raises the risk of particular contaminants… that can cause cancer,” said Dr. Rohan Radhakrishna, Bay Area Air District health officer. According to the findings, the estimated cancer risk is primarily linked to pollutants escaping through small leaks at the facility, while short-term risks are mostly tied to the refinery’s wastewater treatment system. “Everybody deserves to breathe the cleanest air possible… and people are looking to government and science to provide reliable results to make their life safer,” Radhakrishna said. A map presented during the meeting highlighted the highest estimated risks near Point Richmond and the Richmond Parkway. Contra Costa County Supervisor John Gioia said the priority is utilizing the report to drive environmental improvements. “I think this report… helps to understand the health impacts of the refinery,” Gioia said. For lifelong Richmond residents, the data validates long-standing local concerns. “Over the years we’ve heard that Richmond refinery is the highest polluter in the state,” one community member noted during public comment. “I think more than anything it’s how do we reduce the risk? We all have children, we all work here,” said Richmond resident Tania Pulido. Other residents expressed skepticism regarding whether Chevron will implement lasting corrections. “Only way they’ll reduce it is if there’s infrastructure out there to keep on flagging every time they mess up,” said Richmond resident Dshawn Goodwin. Chevron pushed back against the findings, questioning the accuracy of the report in a statement released Monday: “A health-protective assessment should also be accurate. The Air District acknowledges that key assumptions in their draft report may overstate estimated risk. We agree and have identified outdated equipment and assumptions that do not reflect actual operations.” The assessment remains preliminary, with a public comment period open through Nov. 23. If the elevated risk levels are ultimately confirmed, Chevron will be required to develop and execute a compliance plan to reduce them within five years.

headlines.title: Hispanic Heritage Month spotlight: Con Azucar Café owner Alejandra Gonzalez
headlines.description: Con Azucar Café is a national franchise, but it all started with a Bay Area visionary and a dream. Owner Alejandra Gonzalez graduated from Los Gatos High School and attended a vocational school in San Jose. That landed her a job at Tesla, where she ran their new recycling department, eventually overseeing 400 employees. But she wanted more. She decided to quit Tesla and open a Mexican coffee shop with her husband, calling it Con Azucar. It was a gamble. “It is very scary,” Gonzalez said. “We still don’t know what’s on the other side. But it’s a learning process like everything. I think we’ve learned a lot throughout the time.” The gamble has paid off. Con Azucar has become an institution, leading to locations across the Bay Area and franchises in Los Angeles, Nebraska and Texas. Moving forward, one investor has developed a plan to open 100 franchise locations in 10 years in Southern California. Celebrating Hispanic Heritage Sep 15 Art and Culture Sep 15 Hispanic Heritage Month: History, celebrations and why it begins on September 15

headlines.title: 1 killed, 1 seriously injured in Highway 101 crash in San Jose
headlines.description: A 19-year-old man was killed and another was seriously injured in a crash on Highway 101 in San Jose early Sunday, according to the California Highway Patrol. The solo-vehicle crash happened around 2:06 a.m. on northbound Highway 101 at Yerba Buena Road. CHP said a preliminary investigation indicates the driver of a 2013 Ford Fusion lost control of the vehicle while traveling northbound. A 19-year-old passenger from Fairfield was ejected from the vehicle and died from his injuries, according to CHP. The driver, a 19-year-old man from San Mateo, was taken to a hospital with major injuries. CHP said it is not yet known whether alcohol or drugs were factors in the crash. The crash remains under investigation. Anyone with information is asked to contact the San Jose CHP office at 408-961-0900.

headlines.title: Paramount reaches deal with California, other states over Warner merger
headlines.description: The California’s attorney general’s office announced a settlement Monday resolving a 12-state legal challenge to Paramount Skydance’s $110 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, clearing a key hurdle for the transaction. The merger would join together two historic film studios (Paramount and Warner Bros.), two popular streaming platforms (Paramount+ and HBO Max) and two news organizations (CBS News and CNN) under the leadership of 43-year-old mogul David Ellison. The states opposing the deal, led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, sued to block the merger July 13, arguing in a 38-page complaint that it would “extinguish competition” in Hollywood. The terms of the settlement include a pledge by the company to release 30 films per year for the first two years of the deal, followed by 32 films in each of the following three years — or pay a fee for missing that target. Bonta also said that the combined company would invest more than $1 billion in production and film releases in the United States. Paramount is also pledging to establish independent editorial boards overseeing the operations of CNN and CBS News. Also Monday, the Writers’ Guild of America announced it had settled its lawsuit with Paramount. The guild, which is made up of more than 21,000 members, said in its statement that it is still opposed to the deal, but after the states moved to drop their case, it had to “contend with the reality of forging ahead alone.” As part of its settlement terms, the union said Paramount has agreed “to prohibit writer layoffs at CBS News Broadcast for 5 years, and to pay $17.5 million to our health fund along with our attorneys’ fees in the litigation.” Paramount had agreed to freeze the merger until either the antitrust challenge was resolved or June 1, 2027 — whichever came first. Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, who is presiding over the case, had scheduled an antitrust trial for early March. The fee of $30 million per missed film will be paid into health care and retirement trust funds associated with Hollywood unions, such as the Writers Guild, International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees and Directors Guild of America. In a statement Monday, Ellison said, “We are grateful to Attorney General Bonta and his fellow AGs, as well as the WGA, for engaging in good faith to find a path forward to a resolution that serves all parties, and to Governor Newsom for his support throughout this process.” “Our goal has always been to build a stronger Hollywood — one with more stories told, greater choice for consumers and stronger competition,” he added. Shares of both Paramount and Warner soared more than 10% as reports of the settlement circulated early in the day. Additionally, as part of the states’ settlement agreement, “the merged company must conduct negotiations for Paramount basic cable channels independently from negotiations for Warner basic cable channels, preserving the existing competitive dynamic between the companies,” New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport said in a statement. “The merged company will commit $47.5 million in a workforce fund over five years for training and career development for workers who are displaced by the merger,” the statement said. The lawsuit challenging the deal was filed by Bonta and his fellow Democratic attorneys general from Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Washington. They argued that the transaction violated Section 7 of the Clayton Antitrust Act of 1914, a federal law that bars mergers likely to reduce competition. The states said the deal would lessen competition in three areas: wide-release theatrical film distribution, anticipated top-grossing movie distribution and the market for distributing basic cable channels to cable and satellite providers. Paramount rejected those claims, arguing that the states’ suit is “wrong on both the facts and the law” and “one of the weakest merger challenges in modern antitrust history.” Paramount executives had been eager to wrap up the deal as soon as possible partly because the company agreed to pay Warner shareholders a “ticking fee” of 25 cents a share each quarter if the transaction did not close by Sept. 30 — a penalty worth more than $600 million every three months. In August, Paramount’s lawyers asked Martínez-Olguín to require the merger’s legal opponents, which also includes the Writers Guild, to put up a nearly $1.9 billion bond. The money, the company said, would cover the costs of delays caused by the antitrust lawsuit. The Justice Department threw its support behind Paramount’s demand that the opponents should be forced to post a bond as the price of continuing to block the merger. Martínez-Olguín had scheduled a hearing on Paramount’s bond request for Sept. 24. Media Jul 24 Media Jul 13 Hollywood’s mixed views on merger Paramount had already received regulatory clearance from the Justice Department, which approved the deal June 12, and it has touted similar approvals from other foreign territories, including Australia, Canada and China. The deal was given the green light by the European Commission on July 21, which required the company to divest its stake in United International Pictures and not enter any film distribution deals with Universal in the European Economic Area for 10 years. The merger also has the backing of AMC Theatres and Regal Cinemas, the largest movie theater chains in the U.S. by number of locations and screens. But many outspoken actors, writers and producers in Hollywood have rallied behind efforts to block the merger, arguing in an open letter earlier this year that further corporate consolidation of the entertainment industry will “threaten the sustainability of the entire creative community.” Paramount has repeatedly insisted the deal is “lawful, pro-competitive, and will benefit consumers, creators, workers, and the entertainment industry.” The company has argued that big studios face healthy competition from smaller film distribution labels, including recent hitmakers Amazon MGM (“Project Hail Mary”), A24 (“Backrooms”) and Lionsgate (“Michael”). The actors’ union SAG-AFTRA issued a statement shortly after a settlement was reached saying it believes the terms address “some of our deep concerns about production levels and investment in U.S. production” “We will continue to approach our relationship with Paramount with professionalism and the intention to work well together,” SAG-AFTRA President Sean Astin and National Executive Director and chief negotiator Duncan Crabtree-Ireland said in the statement. “We hope that the process of engaging with the attorneys general has impressed upon them the fact that in addition to collective bargaining, our members rely on the law to help protect our interests.. These are the lowest standards that our employers must meet.” On Sunday and Monday, members of the Committee for the First Amendment, a free-speech advocacy group headed by actor Jane Fonda — organized rallies in Oakland, California, outside Bonta’s office, and in New York City, outside state Attorney General Letitia James’ office. Holding signs reading “#BlockTheMerger,” the protesters called on attorneys general from the states suing Paramount to “stay strong” and resist making concessions in negotiations. “We just want to thank everyone for listening, we want people to spread the word and let everyone know: this merger is bad,” said Bruce Cohen, a producer who was among the rally attendees and speakers Monday. “It’s bad for Hollywood, it’s bad for workers, it’s bad for democracy.”
headlines.source: Daniel Arkin, Saba Hamedy and Steve Kopack | NBC News

headlines.title: No evidence injured girl was involved in Redwood City crash, police say
headlines.description: Authorities have found no evidence to back up a report that an injured girl was spotted at the scene of a rollover crash Sunday night in Redwood City, police said. The crash occurred about 10:40 p.m. on northbound U.S. Highway 101 at the overpass north of Woodside Road. The suspect fled the scene on foot, authorities said. Police and California Highway Patrol officers searched the area following a report that a 4- to 5-year-old girl, with blonde or brown hair and a pink jacket, was seen bleeding from the head after the crash. “After a thorough search, no juvenile matching the reported description was located and there is currently no evidence that a child was involved,” police said in an update on Monday morning.

headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot and descriptions from the secretary of state: Proposition 1: Authorizes bonds for housing affordability programs Proposition 2: Increases state’s rainy day fund Proposition 3: Provides permanent funding for schools and healthcare by extending existing tax on high incomes Proposition 4: Repeals prohibition against public funding of election campaigns. Proposition 5: Changes recall election process for statewide officers. Proposition 37: Creates loan program for middle-income buyers of qualified new homes. Proposition 38: Authorizes bonds for immunology medical research. Proposition 39: Prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification. Proposition 40: Imposes one-time tax on certain taxpayers. Proposition 41: Prohibits new state taxes that exclude revenues from state spending limit. Requires audits for new state special taxes. Proposition 42: Prohibits new state personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes. Proposition 43: Limits voters’ ability to raise revenues for local government services. Proposition 44: Requires community health clinics spend 90% of revenue on program services. Proposition 45: Modifies environmental review for certain projects. Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax (not assigned) Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Napa County California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. Measure B in Napa County: Sales tax to fund wildfire prevention and open space preservation. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Napa County and additional election information, visit the Napa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E in Solano County: New tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Solano County and additional election information, visit the Solano County Registrar of Voters website. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. State Assembly District 12: Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward compete in a battle between business and labor. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Sonoma County and additional election information, visit the Sonoma County Registrar of Voters website. headlines.title: San Francisco Fleet Week 2026: Events, schedules, what to know
headlines.description: It’s that time of year again. San Francisco Fleet Week is back. The fall tradition will be highlighted by the Blue Angels screaming across the skies, but there are plenty of other events to experience. Check out the guide below to learn more about Fleet Week events. What is San Francisco Fleet Week? San Francisco Fleet Week is an annual celebration of the nation’s sea services. A multi-day air show, parade of ships and ship tours highlight the weeklong festivities. “San Francisco Fleet Week is an annual public event that honors the contributions of the men and women of the United States Armed Forces while advancing cooperation and knowledge among civilian- and military-based Humanitarian Assistance personnel,” a statement on the event’s website reads. When is San Francisco Fleet Week 2026? Fleet Week is scheduled to take place Sunday, Oct. 4 through Monday, Oct. 12. San Francisco Fleet Week Air Show Head to a location along San Francisco Bay between the Golden Gate Bridge and Alcatraz to catch a thrilling aerial show featuring the Blue Angels, a United Airlines 777, and much more. When: 12 p.m. – 4 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 9, Saturday, Oct. 10 and Sunday, Oct. 11 Lineup and schedule: Stay tuned for detailed information on the airshow lineup and schedule Where: Ticketed seating located at the Marina Green in San Francisco Tickets: Air show tickets are available via the San Francisco Fleet Week website Note: Gates open at 10 a.m. on Friday and 11 a.m. on Saturday and Sunday Bay Area Jan 16 San Francisco Sep 3 San Francisco Fleet Week Parade of Ships Set your eyes on the water near the Golden Gate Bridge to catch the fleet of ships arriving in the Bay, escorted by a San Francisco Fire Department boat shooting water into the air. When: 11 a.m. – 12 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 9 Where: San Francisco Bay waterfront (the parade can be seen from locations along the water between the Golden Gate Bridge and the Bay Bridge) San Francisco Fleet Week Ship Tours Climb aboard various ships to see what it’s like to be a sailor in the U.S. Navy and U.S. Coast Guard. The visiting ships will be announced in late September. headlines.title: San Francisco's first Raising Cane's opens at Fisherman's Wharf
headlines.description: San Francisco’s first Raising Cane’s officially opened its doors at Fisherman’s Wharf on Monday morning, drawing dozens of people hours before the restaurant opened. The first person in line arrived dressed in a Raising Cane’s costume. Kodi Fort, a senior at nearby Galileo High School, got in line around 7:30 a.m. and was one of 20 people who won free Raising Cane’s meals for a year. The Fisherman’s Wharf restaurant marks Raising Cane’s first location in San Francisco, 30 years after the chain was founded in 1996. Not everyone welcomed the new restaurant. A handful of PETA protesters gathered outside to share their opposition to consuming animal products. The protest remained peaceful, and the demonstrators later left. Another Raising Cane’s location is set to open at Stonestown next month.
